title: Internal Control Testing - Tests of Controls
learning_objectives: Understand when and why auditors test internal controls
Distinguish between tests of controls and substantive procedures
Learn the types of tests of controls (inquiry, observation, inspection, reperformance)
Understand how to evaluate control design and operating effectiveness
Apply control testing concepts to IT general controls and application controls
Understand sample sizes and testing frequency for controls
Know how to evaluate and document control deficiencies
Understand integrated audits (SOX 404) and internal control reporting

content.overview: Tests of controls are audit procedures designed to evaluate the operating effectiveness of controls in preventing or detecting material misstatements at the assertion level. While understanding internal control is required for all audits, actually TESTING controls is optional for non-integrated audits and is performed when: (1) the auditor intends to rely on controls to reduce substantive testing, or (2) substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient appropriate evidence (e.g., in highly automated environments). For public companies under SOX 404(b), testing controls is required to opine on internal control effectiveness. This content covers the full scope of control testing from planning through execution, evaluation, and reporting.

when_to_test_controls.description: Testing controls is not always required; auditors must evaluate whether testing is appropriate and efficient
required_situations: Integrated audits (SOX 404) - must test controls to opine on IC effectiveness
Highly automated environments where substantive testing alone is insufficient
When transaction population is so large that testing individual transactions is impractical
When documentation of transactions is inadequate for substantive testing alone
optional_but_beneficial_situations: Controls are well-designed and expected to operate effectively
Testing controls is more efficient than performing extensive substantive testing
High-volume, routine transactions where controls are expected to be effective
Client has sophisticated control environment and activities
Prior experience shows controls are effective
Allows reduction in substantive testing and overall audit efficiency
when_not_to_test_controls: Controls are clearly ineffective or don't exist
Testing controls would be more costly than performing substantive procedures
Small entity with simple operations where substantive approach is more efficient
First-year audit with limited knowledge of client's control system
Low-risk areas where extensive substantive testing is not required anyway
when_to_test_controls.strategic_decision: The decision to test controls is part of the overall audit strategy and depends on efficiency (time and cost) and effectiveness (ability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence). Often a 'combined approach' is used, testing controls in some areas while using a substantive approach in others.

design_effectiveness.definition: Whether the control, individually or in combination with other controls, is capable of effectively preventing, or detecting and correcting, material misstatements
design_effectiveness.evaluation_question: If this control operates as designed, will it prevent or detect material misstatements?
procedures_to_evaluate_design: Inquiry of personnel who perform the control
Inspection of documents and reports used in the control
Walkthrough of transaction from initiation to financial statement inclusion
Review of control documentation (policies, procedures, flowcharts)
Understanding the 'what, who, when, how, and why' of the control
design_effectiveness.timing: Evaluated during risk assessment and understanding of internal control phase
design_effectiveness.outcome: If design is ineffective, no need to test operating effectiveness - control cannot work

operating_effectiveness.definition: Whether the control was applied at relevant times during the period, how it was applied, and by whom
evaluation_questions: Was the control performed consistently throughout the period?
Was it performed correctly each time?
Was it performed by appropriate personnel with proper authority?
Were exceptions properly investigated and resolved?
procedures_to_test_operating_effectivene: Inquiry of personnel (least persuasive alone, must be combined with other procedures)
Observation of control performance (limited to point in time observed)
Inspection of documentation evidencing control performance
Reperformance of the control by the auditor
operating_effectiveness.timing: Performed during fieldwork after design effectiveness is confirmed
operating_effectiveness.sample_based: Tests of operating effectiveness typically involve testing a sample of transactions throughout the period
operating_effectiveness.outcome: Determines whether auditor can assess control risk as low and reduce substantive procedures

design_vs_operating_effectiveness.relationship: A control must be both well-designed AND operating effectively to rely on it. Poor design = don't waste time testing operations. Good design but poor operations = cannot rely on control.

inquiry.description: Asking appropriate personnel about their performance of controls
examples: Ask accounts payable clerk: 'How do you verify that invoices are approved before payment?'
Ask IT manager: 'What is the process for granting system access to new employees?'
Ask supervisor: 'How do you review and approve journal entries?'
inquiry.strengths: Easy to perform, provides understanding of control process, can identify control changes
limitations: Least persuasive evidence - what people say they do vs. what they actually do may differ
Limited to knowledge of person inquired
People may not recall accurately or may overstate compliance
Alone, insufficient for testing operating effectiveness
inquiry.best_practice: ALWAYS combine inquiry with other procedures (inspection, observation, or reperformance)

observation.description: Watching control performance by client personnel
examples: Observe physical inventory count procedures and controls
Observe segregation of duties in cash receipts process
Observe supervisor reviewing and approving transactions
Observe security access controls (badge readers, locked areas)
Observe IT control procedures like backup processes
strengths: Can identify control weaknesses not disclosed through inquiry
Useful for controls that don't leave documentary evidence
limitations: Point-in-time evidence only - control may not operate this way at other times
Hawthorne effect - people may perform better when being observed
Cannot observe controls operating throughout the period
Impractical for controls performed at specific times (month-end close procedures)
observation.best_practice: Useful for understanding controls and confirming design, but must be supplemented with tests throughout the period for operating effectiveness

inspection.description: Examining documents and records for evidence that controls operated
examples: Inspect purchase orders for proper approval signatures
Review system-generated exception reports and evidence of follow-up
Examine bank reconciliations for preparer and reviewer signatures and dates
Inspect time cards for supervisor approval
Review credit approval documentation for new customers
Examine access logs showing authorized personnel made changes
Inspect board minutes for evidence of oversight
Review audit committee meeting minutes
strengths: Provides evidence of control performance throughout the period
Can be sampled to cover entire audit period
Can be performed on sample basis to draw conclusions about population
limitations: Only useful when controls generate documentation
Documents can be forged or falsified
Presence of signature doesn't prove control was performed effectively
Some automated controls don't leave visible evidence
inspection.best_practice: Examine documentation from throughout the period; look beyond signatures to assess whether control was truly performed

reperformance.description: Auditor independently executes control procedure to verify it produces expected result
examples: Recalculate interest accruals to verify automated calculation controls
Re-perform three-way match (PO, receiving report, invoice) to verify system logic
Recalculate depreciation to test automated controls
Re-run edit checks and validation routines to verify they work properly
Recalculate commission payments to verify calculation accuracy
Re-match shipping documents to sales invoices to verify billing controls
Test access controls by attempting unauthorized access
strengths: Most persuasive evidence for controls that involve calculations or processing
Provides direct evidence that control works as intended
Can detect subtle errors in control performance
Verifies not just that control was performed, but that it was performed correctly
limitations: Time-consuming and may not be cost-effective for all controls
May require special skills (e.g., IT knowledge for automated controls)
Still performed on sample basis, not entire population
Some controls are not amenable to reperformance (judgment-based controls)
reperformance.best_practice: Most reliable test of operating effectiveness; use for key automated controls and calculation controls

combination_approach.description: Use multiple types of tests for comprehensive evidence
typical_approach: Inquiry - understand how control is supposed to work
Observation - watch control being performed to confirm understanding
Inspection - examine evidence of control performance across the period
Reperformance - independently execute control for key calculations or automated controls
combination_approach.example: For purchase approval control: (1) Inquire about approval process and limits, (2) Observe supervisor approving a purchase requisition, (3) Inspect sample of 25 purchase orders for approval signatures throughout year, (4) Reperform check of whether purchases exceed approval limits

step_1_identify_controls_to_test.description: Select which controls to test based on relevance to assertions and efficiency
considerations: Controls relevant to assertions with significant risk of material misstatement
Key controls vs. redundant controls (test key controls only)
Manual vs. automated controls (automated controls may require less frequent testing)
Controls that, if effective, would allow most reduction in substantive testing
step_1_identify_controls_to_test.focus_on_key_controls: Don't test every control; focus on key controls that have the greatest impact on reducing assessed control risk

step_2_determine_sample_size.description: Decide how many instances of the control to test
factors_affecting_sample_size: Frequency of control performance (daily, weekly, monthly, annually)
Importance of control to reducing risk
Expected deviation rate (higher expected deviations = larger sample)
Prior experience with control (effective in prior years = may allow smaller sample)

automated_controls.description: Once an automated control is verified to be functioning, it will process all transactions identically
automated_controls.typical_approach: Test 1-2 instances to verify control is programmed correctly, plus test IT general controls to ensure unauthorized changes can't be made
automated_controls.key_point: Automated controls are either working 100% or not working at all (no partial effectiveness)

manual_controls_daily.typical_sample: 25-40 items, depending on risk and expected deviation rate
manual_controls_daily.coverage: Should include items from throughout the period

manual_controls_weekly.coverage: Several from each month or quarter

manual_controls_monthly.coverage: Often test all or most instances when frequency is low

manual_controls_annually_or_quarterly.coverage: Must test each occurrence when frequency is very low

step_2_determine_sample_size.professional_judgment: Sample sizes are not prescribed by standards; require professional judgment based on circumstances

step_3_select_sample_items.description: Choose which specific items to test from the population
selection_methods: Random selection - every item has equal chance of selection
Systematic selection - select every nth item
Haphazard selection - select without conscious bias (not truly random)
Stratified selection - divide population into subgroups and sample each
Judgmental selection - select items most likely to contain errors (for design testing)
step_3_select_sample_items.timing_coverage: Ensure selection covers the entire audit period, not just convenient periods
step_3_select_sample_items.avoid_bias: Selection method should not introduce bias favoring or excluding certain types of items

step_4_perform_tests.description: Execute the planned tests of controls procedures
execution_considerations: Document all testing performed and results
Investigate nature and cause of exceptions
Determine whether exception represents control failure or other cause
Be alert for indicators of override or bypassed controls

step_5_evaluate_results.description: Assess whether controls operated effectively based on test results

deviation_rate.description: Percentage of sample items where control did not operate as expected
deviation_rate.example: 3 deviations out of 30 items tested = 10% deviation rate
assessment: 0% deviation rate = control operated effectively (subject to sampling risk)
1-5% deviation rate = generally acceptable, evaluate nature of deviations
5-10% deviation rate = investigate causes, may indicate control deficiency
> 10% deviation rate = control not operating effectively, likely deficiency
deviation_rate.important_caveat: Not just about quantity - even one deviation could be significant if it's material or indicates fraud

nature_of_deviations: Isolated human error vs. systemic problem
Pattern (e.g., all in one month, all by one person)
Whether deviation could result in material misstatement

step_5_evaluate_results.assessment_conclusion: Based on deviation rate, nature, and cause, conclude whether control can be relied upon to reduce assessed control risk

required_documentation: Investigation of deviations and root causes
Impact on assessed control risk and planned substantive procedures

it_controls_testing.overview: IT controls are increasingly important as businesses rely on technology. IT controls are divided into IT General Controls (ITGCs) and Application Controls.

it_general_controls.description: Controls over the IT environment that support the effective functioning of application controls

access_controls.purpose: Prevent unauthorized access to systems, programs, and data
key_controls: Physical access to data centers and servers
testing_procedures: Inspect user access lists and compare to authorized personnel
Test password policies and lockout settings
Review process for granting and removing access
Test whether terminated employees' access was disabled timely
Attempt to access system with unauthorized credentials (controlled test)
Review logs of privileged user activity

program_change_controls.purpose: Ensure only authorized, tested changes are made to programs and systems
key_controls: Testing of changes in non-production environment
Segregation of duties (developers don't have production access)
Management approval before promoting to production
testing_procedures: Select sample of program changes made during year
Inspect change requests for proper approval
Verify changes were tested before production implementation
Confirm developer access to production is restricted
Review change logs and compare to approved changes
Verify emergency change procedures include after-the-fact approval

computer_operations.purpose: Ensure systems are operated securely and reliably
key_controls: Disaster recovery and business continuity planning
testing_procedures: Inspect backup logs and test restore procedures
Review disaster recovery plan and test results
Verify automated jobs run as scheduled
Review incident logs and resolution
Test whether monitoring alerts are functioning

system_software_controls.purpose: Ensure operating systems, databases, and system software are secure and properly configured
key_controls: Segregation of duties in system administration
testing_procedures: Review patch management logs
Verify anti-virus is active and updated
Inspect firewall rules and security settings
Test whether system configurations meet standards
Review administrator access and segregation of duties

it_general_controls.importance: ITGCs are foundational - if ITGCs are weak, application controls cannot be relied upon (even if application controls appear effective, unauthorized changes could compromise them)
it_general_controls.testing_frequency: ITGCs are typically tested annually; if effective in prior year and no changes, may require less extensive testing

application_controls.description: Controls within application systems that process transactions

input_controls.purpose: Ensure data entered into system is complete, accurate, and authorized
examples: Edit checks (field validation - e.g., numeric fields only accept numbers)
Completeness checks (required fields must be populated)
Validity checks (customer number must exist in customer master file)
Range checks (overtime hours can't exceed 20 per week)
Reasonableness checks (purchase price can't be negative)
Authorization controls (manager approval required for orders > $10,000)
Batch controls (total number of records and dollar amounts match)
Duplicate detection (prevent duplicate invoice entry)
input_controls.testing: Reperform control by entering test transactions with errors and verify system rejects them

processing_controls.purpose: Ensure data is processed completely and accurately
examples: Calculations (interest, depreciation, commissions computed correctly)
Matching (three-way match of PO, receiving report, invoice)
Sequence checks (all invoice numbers accounted for)
Run-to-run totals (ensure data not lost between processing steps)
processing_controls.testing: Reperform calculations or matching procedures to verify accuracy

output_controls.purpose: Ensure output is complete, accurate, and distributed appropriately
examples: Reconciliations of output to input
Review of exception reports
Output distribution controls (sensitive reports go only to authorized users)
Report retention and archive controls
output_controls.testing: Inspect exception reports and evidence of review; verify reconciliations performed

application_controls.automated_nature: Application controls are usually automated, so once verified to be functioning, they operate consistently (subject to ITGCs ensuring no unauthorized changes)

reliance_on_it_controls.requirement: To rely on automated application controls, auditor must test both the application control AND the ITGCs supporting it
reliance_on_it_controls.relationship: Strong ITGCs × Effective application controls = Reliance. Weak ITGCs = Cannot rely on application controls regardless of how effective they appear
reliance_on_it_controls.specialist_involvement: Complex IT environments often require IT audit specialists to test controls

evaluating_control_deficiencies.description: When controls don't operate effectively, auditors must evaluate the severity of the deficiency

control_deficiency.definition: A control is missing or not designed/operating effectively to prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis
control_deficiency.assessment: Less severe; unlikely to result in material misstatement individually or in combination

significant_deficiency.definition: A deficiency, or combination of deficiencies, that is less severe than a material weakness yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance
indicators: Could reasonably result in more than inconsequential misstatement
Multiple control deficiencies in same area
Deficiency wasn't corrected timely after being identified
significant_deficiency.reporting: Must be communicated in writing to management and those charged with governance

material_weakness.definition: A deficiency, or combination of deficiencies, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity's financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis
indicators: Could result in material misstatement of financial statements
Fraud by senior management (even if immaterial amount)
Restatement of previously issued financial statements for material error
Identification by auditor of material misstatement not detected by entity's controls
Ineffective internal audit function in complex entity
material_weakness.reporting: Must be communicated in writing to management and those charged with governance; for public companies, results in adverse opinion on internal control effectiveness (SOX 404)

evaluation_factors.likelihood: How likely is it that the deficiency could result in a misstatement?
evaluation_factors.magnitude: How large would the potential misstatement be?
considerations: Nature of account and assertion affected
Volume and dollar amount of transactions

compensating_controls.description: Other controls that reduce the risk associated with the deficiency
compensating_controls.example: If control over purchase approvals is weak, compensating control might be strong accounts payable reconciliation that would detect unauthorized purchases
compensating_controls.assessment: Presence of compensating controls may reduce severity classification, but doesn't eliminate the deficiency

material_weaknesses_and_significant_defi: Must be communicated in writing to management and those charged with governance
Must be communicated timely (by date of auditor's report for non-public, earlier for public companies)
Communication should describe deficiency and its actual/potential effects
Should include management's response if received
all_deficiencies: Auditor may communicate to management (not required unless MW or SD)

integrated_audits_sox_404.overview: Public companies must have management assess internal control effectiveness (SOX 404(a)) and auditor opine on it (SOX 404(b) for larger companies)

management_assessment_404a.requirement: Management must assess and report on internal control over financial reporting effectiveness
management_assessment_404a.framework: Usually COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework
management_assessment_404a.auditor_evaluation: Auditor must evaluate management's assessment process but doesn't opine on it separately

auditor_attestation_404b.requirement: For accelerated and large accelerated filers, auditor must opine on IC effectiveness
auditor_attestation_404b.integrated_with_financial_statement_audi: AS 2201 requires integrated audit approach - not two separate engagements

opinion_types.unqualified: IC is effective in all material respects (no material weaknesses)
opinion_types.adverse: One or more material weaknesses exist; IC is not effective
opinion_types.qualified: Scope limitation prevented testing; unusual in practice

testing_requirements: Must test design and operating effectiveness of all controls relevant to assertions for material accounts
Must test controls over relevant assertions
Sample sizes must be sufficient to support opinion on IC (more extensive than when just reducing substantive testing)
Must test controls as of year-end (not interim)
Must re-test controls annually (prior year results provide some, but not sufficient, evidence)

differences_from_non_integrated_audits.scope: Integrated audits require testing ALL relevant controls; non-integrated audits may choose to test only selected controls
differences_from_non_integrated_audits.objective: Integrated audits opine on IC; non-integrated audits use control testing to reduce substantive work
differences_from_non_integrated_audits.extent: Integrated audits require more extensive testing to support separate opinion
differences_from_non_integrated_audits.reporting: Integrated audits issue separate IC opinion; non-integrated communicate deficiencies but don't opine on overall IC
differences_from_non_integrated_audits.cost: Integrated audits are significantly more costly due to additional IC testing requirements

key_concepts: Testing controls is optional for non-integrated audits (done when efficient or when substantive alone is insufficient)
Must test both design AND operating effectiveness to rely on controls
Inquiry alone is insufficient - must combine with inspection, observation, or reperformance
Automated controls need less frequent testing but require ITGC testing
Material weaknesses must be communicated in writing to governance
For integrated audits (SOX 404), testing controls is required
Deviation rate affects assessed control risk and required substantive testing
common_exam_scenarios: Given control and asked which test procedure is most appropriate
Given deviation rate and asked to assess control effectiveness
Distinguish between design and operating effectiveness
Identify which deficiency severity level applies
Determine sample size for control testing given frequency
Identify when testing controls is required vs. optional
formula_and_calculations: Deviation rate = Number of deviations ÷ Sample size
Higher expected deviation rate → Larger sample needed
Manual daily control: Sample typically 25-40 items
Manual monthly control: Sample typically all 12 or 8-12 months

practice_problems.title: Control Testing Scenario - Purchase-to-Pay Cycle
practice_problems.scenario:
You are auditing the purchases and accounts payable for Mountain Manufacturing Corp. During your understanding of internal control, you identified the following key controls in the purchase-to-pay cycle:

Control 1: All purchase requisitions over $5,000 must be approved by department manager before a purchase order is created. Approval is evidenced by manager's signature on requisition.

Control 2: The ERP system automatically performs three-way matching (purchase order, receiving report, and vendor invoice) and will not create a payable unless all three documents match in quantity and price (within 5% tolerance).

Control 3: Every month, the accounts payable supervisor reconciles the accounts payable sub-ledger to the general ledger accounts payable control account. Reconciliation is documented and reviewed by the controller.

You have decided to test these controls to potentially reduce substantive testing.
required: Part A: For each control, determine the type(s) of test procedures you would perform and explain why.
Part B: Determine appropriate sample sizes for testing each control's operating effectiveness.

Part C: You tested Control 1 by examining 30 purchase requisitions and found 3 instances where requisitions over $5,000 were not approved by a manager before the PO was created. What is the deviation rate? How should you evaluate this result?
Part D: For Control 2 (automated three-way match), what additional testing is necessary beyond testing the application control itself?

summary: Testing internal controls is a critical component of many audits, allowing auditors to assess control risk and potentially reduce substantive testing. While optional for non-integrated audits, control testing becomes required when substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient evidence or when conducting integrated audits under SOX 404. Effective control testing requires evaluating both design effectiveness (is the control capable of preventing/detecting misstatements?) and operating effectiveness (did it actually operate throughout the period?). The four types of control tests - inquiry, observation, inspection, and reperformance - each provide different levels of evidence, with inquiry being least persuasive and reperformance being most persuasive. IT controls require special consideration, with IT general controls providing the foundation for reliable automated application controls. Control deficiencies must be evaluated and classified as control deficiencies, significant deficiencies, or material weaknesses based on their potential to result in material misstatement. For CPA candidates, understanding when and how to test controls, how to evaluate results, and how to respond to control deficiencies is essential for success on the AUD exam.
